newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Zaire rebels block UN mission to probe massacres.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels block UN mission to probe massacres.

text.p: A U.N. team and forensic experts hoping to investigate alleged rebel massacres in east Zaire were stuck in Rwanda for the third straight day on Tuesday as Tutsi-led rebels dragged their feet over granting access.

Scepticism grew over the fate of the mission, ordered by the top United Nations human rights body, after U.N. officials made first direct contact with the evasive rebels on Monday but apparently failed to win guarantees.

"The mission has not received the necessary assurances on access to all sites they would like to visit, on security of witnesses and on their freedom of movement," U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut told a news briefing in Geneva.
"They're losing time. The team can't go into Zaire without a green light," she said. "So far, we only have amber light."
The team, in Rwanda since Saturday, had planned to go to Zaire after a Sunday meeting between rebels and two U.N. rights experts in the eastern town of Lumumbashi, which was delayed.
"The advance team still needs to clear the programme, activities and places the members of the mission want to see," a U.N. source told Reuters. "We are hoping for movement today."
Time is tight, with the mission facing a June 30 deadline to report to the U.N. General Assembly on its findings on widespread massacre allegations and the outcome of excavations.
The mission faces many uncertainties and it is unclear whether it will be able to accomplish much.
The rebels who control more than half of Zaire have objected to the team's composition and its methods of work.
The team faces logistical problems in chaotic Zaire. The forensic work could be complicated by the current rainy season. Witnesses may refuse to talk for fear of their lives.
The commission of inquiry, established on April 15, seeks to probe alleged massacres by the rebels after they shelled and overran Rwandan refugee camps in Goma region late last year.
U.N. rights investigator for Zaire, Roberto Garreton, last month accused the rebels of continuing massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees and civilians in the east.
Garreton said witness reports spoke of as many as 50,000 Hutu refugees and civilians killed by the rebels.
Last week, he said that fresh charges of rebel killings of Hutu refugees at refugee camps south of the eastern city of Kisangani should also be a priority for the mission.

Washington said last week there were increasingly credible and "increasingly shocking reports" of killings of refugees around Kisangani and other rebel-held areas and urged the rebels to give the U.N. team full access to suspected killing sites.
This is the first U.N. rights mission to the troubled region where centuries-old ethnic hatred between the majority Hutus and minority Tutsis has repeatedly exploded into bloodshed.

The Hutus are the rump of two million Rwandans who fled to Zaire after Tutsi rebels ended the Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. Many among them killed or watched others kill in one of the worst mass slaughters of the century.
Apart from Garreton, the U.N. team has Waly Bacre N'Diaye, U.N. rights investigator on extrajudicial, summary and arbitrary executions, and Jonas Foli, a rights expert on disappearances.
It is accompanied by five forensic experts of the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team who have shortlisted fewer than 10 grave sites for random excavation out of some 40 identified.
